name: Thunder Egg
mineralClass: Rock (rhyolite nodule filled with agate or quartz)
luster: Dull outside, waxy to vitreous inside
spiritual: Reminds that inner beauty is hidden
Connects to storm and earth energy
physical: Traditionally linked to vitality and lively energy
Associated with a feeling of renewal
Kept nearby by many for motivation and cheer
summary: A thunder egg is a rough volcanic nodule hiding agate or quartz inside, a stone of surprise, creativity and hidden potential in crystal lore.
intro: A thunder egg looks like an ordinary lumpy rock until it is cracked or sawn open. Inside, the dull brown or grey rhyolite shell often reveals a star-shaped or round cavity filled with agate, jasper, opal or quartz, in banded colors that can be blue, red, pink or smoky white. Every egg is a surprise, and that is the main joy of collecting them. They range from marble-sized to the size of a basketball. Cut halves are sold as bookends and display pieces, and smaller polished pieces are made into pendants. Few stones fit the feeling of cracking open a present so well.
history: Thunder eggs are the state rock of Oregon, and the name is credited to Native American folklore that explained them as missiles thrown by thunder spirits hurling stones from mountain tops during storms. Depending on the retelling, the stones were pitched between rival thunder beings living on Mount Hood and Mount Jefferson. Geologically, they form in volcanic ash and lava flows, when gas bubbles in the rhyolite are later filled with silica-rich water that slowly crystallizes into agate or quartz. Rockhounds have dug them for generations in the Oregon high desert, and similar nodules are found in Mexico, Australia and Madagascar.
meaning: Thunder eggs stand for hidden potential and the courage to look inside. Practitioners read the plain outer shell and the glittering core as a reminder that many of our strengths are not obvious at first. They are linked to the root, sacral and solar plexus, and used by people who feel creatively blocked or unsure of themselves. The storm folklore adds a flavor of electric motivation, and many keep a thunder egg to inspire bold starts. Because each one is a gamble, they also suit rituals around trusting the process. Traditionally the stone is associated with lively energy, playful curiosity and a renewed sense of vitality.
howToUse: Keep a cut thunder egg on a desk or studio table to encourage creativity, or gift a small one to someone starting a new chapter. Rest your palm on the polished interior while you set an intention, tracing the bands with your fingertip as a kind of walking meditation. Whole, uncut eggs are great for ritual: crack one open together with a friend as a symbolic celebration. In a grid, place a half at the center to represent potential waiting to be revealed. Small polished pieces make good pocket stones for days that need a spark.
care: Thunder eggs are hard and durable, so they handle a rinse in lukewarm water and a brush to remove dust from cavities. Dry them thoroughly. Cleanse them with moonlight, smoke, sound or by burying briefly in earth, and charge in sunlight. Handle open cavities gently, since tiny crystals can chip. Store them away from softer stones, and wrap rough exteriors so they do not scratch other pieces.
identify: Genuine thunder eggs have a rough, bumpy, brown or grey outer rind of rhyolite with a sharp contact line to the agate or quartz inside. The interior should show natural banding and cavities rather than uniform, bright, painted color. Dyed agate halves sometimes sold as thunder eggs show intense, unnatural hues and a lack of the outer rind. Weight and the natural irregular shape are good clues, and reputable sellers will name the locality.

faq.q: What is inside a thunder egg?
faq.a: Inside a thunder egg you usually find agate, jasper, opal or quartz that filled an open cavity in volcanic rock. The inside can be banded, star-shaped or hollow with tiny crystals, and every one is different.

faq.q: Why are they called thunder eggs?
faq.a: Native American folklore described them as stones thrown by thunder spirits during storms. The name stuck, and rockhounds and collectors have used it ever since for these lumpy volcanic nodules.

faq.q: What is a thunder egg good for in crystal lore?
faq.a: Crystal lovers use thunder eggs for creativity, motivation and hidden potential. The plain shell and bright core is a reminder that surprising strengths can sit just beneath the surface.
